claims.text: TaNbHfZrTi-type high-entropy alloys can be superconducting.
The TaNbHfZrTi-type superconducting alloy has a disordered bcc structure.
The specified TaNbHfZrTi alloy is a single-phase material.
High mixing entropy favors crystallization of HEAs in simple structures such as bcc.
High configurational disorder creates local lattice distortions in high-entropy superconducting alloys.
Local lattice distortions alter the phonon spectrum or phonon density of states.
The distortion-induced phonon changes enhance electron–phonon coupling.
Electron–phonon coupling modified by configurational disorder changes the superconducting transition temperature.
Spatial variation in distortion-enhanced electron–phonon coupling broadens the superconducting transition.
Superconducting HEAs generally exhibit conventional BCS-like pairing with intermediate-to-strong coupling.
The degree of disorder can affect superconductivity.
Electron count is an important parameter affecting superconductivity in these alloy systems.
Increasing mixing entropy has been observed together with a reduction in Tc in superconducting HEAs.
The microscopic role of disorder in superconducting HEAs remains unresolved.
A high-disorder HEA should have either a higher Tc or a broader heat-capacity or resistivity transition than a low-disorder baseline with similar electron count and bcc structure.
Annealing or compositional tuning can produce a binary or ternary bcc baseline with reduced configurational disorder while retaining a comparable average electron count.
Holding electron count, crystal structure, crystallinity, pressure, and strain constant would isolate configurational disorder as the cause of superconducting differences.
Tunneling spectroscopy or a related technique can provide electron–phonon coupling parameters for the proposed comparison.

contradictions.description: The boundary requires configurational disorder to be the only significant difference, but the proposed HEA-versus-binary-or-ternary comparison necessarily changes elemental identity and compositional complexity; matching only average electron count and bcc structure does not ensure that all other relevant variables are controlled.

The prediction is disjunctive—either higher Tc or broader transition would count as confirmation—whereas the falsification rule jointly compares Tc, width, and coupling. A sample could satisfy one predicted branch while also meeting an ambiguously defined part of the falsification condition.
